sections.h: Paul's chapter on the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15)
sections.b: Paul's longest argument is about the resurrection. He recites the early creed (Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, appeared to Peter, the Twelve, five hundred, James, all the apostles and last of all to Paul), and then argues that denying the resurrection of the dead cancels Christ's own rising, the preaching, the faith and the forgiveness of sins. Christ is the firstfruits, the dead will rise in order, death is the last enemy, and at the last trumpet the living will be changed. The Old Testament lines he uses are Genesis 2:7, Psalm 8, Psalm 110, Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14.
sections.refs: 1 Corinthians 15:3; 1 Corinthians 15:12; 1 Corinthians 15:20; 1 Corinthians 15:26; 1 Corinthians 15:52; Isaiah 25:8; Hosea 13:14

common: Paul's list of appearances in 15:3-8 is among the earliest Christian statements about the resurrection, and most scholars date its formula within a few years of the crucifixion.
uncommon: Some scholars hold that the appearances were visions and not an empty tomb (a view that most commentators reject as inconsistent with Paul's word for 'raised'.

sections.b: Paul calls Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20, 23). The first sheaf of the harvest, waved before the LORD, made the rest of the harvest ready for use (Leviticus 23:10-11); in the same way the rising of Christ is the first part of the same harvest, the resurrection of the dead. In the same letter Stephanas's household are "the firstfruits of Achaia" (16:15), the first converts of a region.

Paul sets two men side by side: "as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ" (15:22), the first man a living being (Genesis 2:7) and the last Adam a life-giving spirit (15:45), the first from the earth and made of dust, the second from heaven (15:47). Believers have worn the image of the man of dust and will wear the image of the heavenly one (15:49). He does not decide whether Adam is a single man or a figure for humanity.
sections.refs: 1 Corinthians 15:22; 1 Corinthians 15:45; 1 Corinthians 15:47; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 5:3; Romans 5:12

sections.b: Paul calls the dead in Christ those who have "fallen asleep" (15:6, 18, 20) and says the living will not all "sleep" (15:51). The word is a gentle word for death. The same Paul says elsewhere that to leave the body is to be with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). The churches read the two together in different ways, from conscious waiting to an unconscious sleep, and the card on 15:35-54 sets them out.

"Listen, I am telling you a mystery: not all of us will sleep, but all of us will be changed." The secret God now reveals is that the living and the dead are alike to be changed at the last trumpet, so that what decays puts on what cannot decay (15:51-53). The same word marks the wisdom Paul speaks to the mature in 2:7 and the plan for Israel in Romans 11:25.

sections.h: The Son put under the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24-28)
sections.b: Paul says that Christ must reign until all enemies are under his feet, and that when all things are put under him, "the Son himself will also be put under the One who put all things under him, so that God may be all in all." Trinitarian churches read this as the Son's role as mediator and as man; groups that teach a lesser Son (Jehovah's Witnesses, historic Unitarians) read it as a sign of a Son lower than God. The creed of Constantinople (381) says of Christ "his kingdom will have no end."

Paul tells of a moment when the dead will be raised and the living changed "at the last trumpet." Together with 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 it is one of the two main passages for the doctrine of the rapture. Dispensationalists read it as the church caught up before the tribulation, others as the one return of Christ at the end.

Paul speaks of Christ's "coming" (parousia) when those who belong to him will rise (15:23), of the end when he hands the kingdom to the Father (15:24), and of the last trumpet (15:52). He ends the letter with the Aramaic prayer "Marana tha", "Our Lord, come" (16:22).

The second "all" of 15:22 ("all will be made alive in Christ") is read by most churches as all who belong to Christ (15:23). Origen and Gregory of Nyssa have been read as hoping that all creatures are in the end restored (15:28); the church condemned a form of Origen's teaching in the 500s. The card on 1 Corinthians 15 sets the churches side by side.

Paul lists "the Twelve" (15:5) and, after James, "all the apostles" (15:7), a wider group than the Twelve. He counts himself last, "as to one born at the wrong time," and "the least of the apostles," because he persecuted the church of God (15:8-9). His claim to the title rests on having seen the risen Lord.

sections.h: Paul the persecutor and apostle (1 Corinthians 15:8-10)
sections.b: Paul says he is the least of the apostles and unfit to be called one, since he persecuted the church of God, yet "by God's grace I am what I am" and "I toiled more than all of them" (15:9-10). He describes his daily dangers at Ephesus (15:30-32) and signs the letter with his own hand (16:21).

The earliest creed Paul quotes says "Christ died for our sins, in line with the Scriptures." The preposition "for" is the starting point of every later theory of the atonement. Paul adds that if Christ was not raised, the Corinthians are "still in your sins" (15:17): the forgiveness is tied to the resurrection.

Paul tells the Corinthians to follow the order he gave the churches of Galatia: on the first day of the week each is to put something aside at home, so that no collections have to be made when he comes. He will send those the church approves, with letters, to carry the gift to Jerusalem, and will go along if it seems worthwhile. This is the first mention of the fund; 2 Corinthians 8 and 9 and Romans 15:25-32 return to it.
sections.refs: 1 Corinthians 16:1; 1 Corinthians 16:2; 1 Corinthians 16:3; Galatians 2:10; Romans 15:26; Acts 24:17

sections.b: Paul's rule for the Jerusalem collection is proportion, not a fixed tenth: each is to set aside, on the first day of the week, whatever he has had success earning. He does not mention the tithe of the law. Churches differ on whether the tithe still binds; the card on 1 Corinthians 16 sets them out.

The collection for the saints in Jerusalem is the New Testament's best-known organized act of giving between churches: planned, saved weekly, handled by delegates the givers approve, and carried with letters (1 Corinthians 16:1-4; 2 Corinthians 8:18-21).

sections.h: 'The first day of the week' (1 Corinthians 16:2)
sections.b: Paul's instruction to put money aside "on the first day of the week" is one of the New Testament's first hints of Sunday as a regular day for the church (compare Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). Whether it says the believers met that day, or only fixed a weekly date for saving at home, is debated, and so is what the churches draw from it for the Sabbath.

Paul ends the letter with the Aramaic words Marana tha after the line "If anyone does not love the Lord, that person is to be accursed." The words can be divided as "Our Lord, come!" (a prayer) or "Our Lord has come" (a statement). The Didache ends its Lord's Supper prayers with them (10:6), which has led some to see 16:22 as a call spoken at the Lord's Supper. They are the clearest sign that the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers prayed to Jesus as "Lord".

sections.h: Ephesus as the place of 1 Corinthians
sections.b: Paul writes 1 Corinthians from Ephesus and plans to stay "until Pentecost" because "a door has opened to me, a great one and a productive one, and there are many opponents" (16:8-9). He says he "fought with wild beasts at Ephesus" (15:32), and sends greetings from the churches of Asia and from Aquila and Prisca (16:19).

sections.h: People of Corinth in the closing chapter
sections.b: The church's go-betweens are named in the last chapter: Stephanas, whose household were the firstfruits of Achaia and devoted themselves to serving the saints, and his companions Fortunatus and Achaicus, who refreshed Paul's spirit (16:15-18). Paul asks the Corinthians to honor such people.

Paul calls Apollos "our brother," says he urged him many times to visit Corinth with the brothers, and reports that it was not at all his wish to go now. The Greek leaves open whose wish it was. Paul treats him as a free colleague, which helps answer the picture of rival parties in 1:12.

sections.h: Aquila and Prisca at Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19)
sections.b: When Paul writes from Ephesus, Aquila and Prisca are there with a church that meets in their house. They had met Paul in Corinth after Claudius expelled Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2) and were back in Rome by the time of Romans 16:3-5.

"The church that meets in their house" (16:19) shows the form of the early church: a gathering in a large home. Corinth had several (1:16; 16:15), and Paul asks the church to honor those who labor, as Stephanas's household did (16:16).

sections.h: Pentecost as the date of 1 Corinthians
sections.b: Paul says he will stay at Ephesus "until Pentecost" (16:8), the Jewish Feast of Weeks fifty days after Passover. The mention puts the writing of the letter in spring, before that feast.

The letter ends with a curse on anyone who does not love the Lord, in the same word (anathema) Paul uses of a false gospel in Galatians 1:8-9. Whether it is a ban from the community or a handing over to God's judgment is debated.

Paul answers "With what sort of body do they come?" with seeds, many kinds of flesh, the glory of the sun, moon and stars, and two Adams. The body is sown in decay, dishonor and weakness and raised in what cannot decay, in glory and power; sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body. "Spiritual" means ruled by God's Spirit, not made of spirit, on the reading of most Fathers and commentators; a few scholars argue that Paul thought of spirit as a fine kind of matter.

common: Most commentators take 'spiritual body' as a real body transformed by the Spirit.
uncommon: A minority (including Dale Martin and Troels Engberg-Pedersen) argue that Paul, like the Stoics, pictured the spirit as a very fine material.

sections.b: Paul asks what those who are baptized for the dead will do if the dead are not raised. He neither approves nor condemns the practice. Readings include proxy baptism of the living for the dead (Chrysostom attributes it to the Marcionites, Epiphanius to the Cerinthians; Tertullian reads "the dead" as the body and treats the custom as Paul's argument), baptism in hope of rejoining dead believers, a picture of dying with Christ, or a local custom of Corinth. The Latter-day Saints are the best-known body that practices baptism for the dead today.
